unit.title: Harness Engineering Fundamentals
unit.moc: agent = model + harness — the 8 components — harness beats model — failure stats — tribunal's map — sensors proven

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint 2 — gate
checkpoint.prompt: Classify a fictional system against the 8 harness components and say which layer the tribunal itself was weakest in.

facts.text: An agent is two parts: the model that reasons, and the harness — everything wrapped around it. The harness decides what the model sees, what it can do, and how it recovers from mistakes.

This split matters because harness engineering is its own discipline, separate from prompt engineering and model selection. Keep the same model and you still get very different behavior by changing the harness.
Same model, different harness: swap the guides and sensors and the same reasoning engine will refuse a bad edit it used to make, or catch its own error before Record.
Learners often say 'the model is the agent'. It is not — the model is one component. In the learn path, the checkpoint that gates this unit is the harness's verification layer turned into a quiz.

options: everything around the model — what it sees, what it can do, how it recovers

exercises.prompt: Harness engineering is the same thing as model selection.

facts.text: A harness is inventoried in eight components: guides, sensors, memory/state, tool-execution, guardrails, loop controller, verification, and failure handler. Each owns a job in the agent's life cycle.

Guides are the feedforward layer (`AGENTS.md`, conventions) — they tell the model how to behave before it acts. Sensors are the feedback layer (linters, type checks, LLM-as-judge) — they tell it how it did after.
Guardrails encode policy — for example the tribunal's structural rules like `DeepSeek-once` and `MAX_LANES=4`. They are the 'no' the model cannot overrule, distinct from a sensor that merely reports.

Verification is the most-skipped layer. Teams ship sensors that only confirm output is non-empty and call it done — but non-empty is a trivial check; real verification proves the thing actually works.

In the learn path, the `complete` exercise where you fill in memory/state and verification is exactly this inventory — and the checkpoint asks you to map a fictional system onto these eight components.

exercises.prompt: Match each component to its role.
Which component is the FEEDFORWARD layer?
The 8 components: guides, sensors, ___, tool-execution, guardrails, loop controller, ___, failure handler.

facts.text: Improving the harness around a model beats swapping the model. Same engine, better guardrails, sensors, and loops, and the agent gets markedly better.
Cited literature: harness changes delivered 5–14 benchmark points and ~20% fewer tokens on the SAME model. The gain comes from the wrapper, not a bigger brain.
Manus rewrote its harness 5 times in 6 months while keeping the same model — proof that the harness, not the model version, is the lever.
The tempting move is to 'just buy a bigger model'. The literature says that spends tokens without the discipline a good harness gives you for free.

options: 5–14 benchmark points and −20% tokens on the same model

exercises.prompt: Manus rewrote its harness ___ in 6 months with the same model.
The moral of this lesson is:
options: improve the harness around the model

facts.text: The field is brutal: ~88% of agent projects never reach production. Building an agent is easy; operating one reliably is not.
~27% of failures trace to data quality — the agent reasons on bad or unverified inputs, so even a perfect model produces a wrong result.

The most-skipped layer is verification: 'models say done when they're not done', and a sensor that only checks for non-empty output passes trivially. That gap is why projects stall right after the demo.
A common misread is that these numbers argue for a bigger model. They do not — they argue for verification and data quality, the harness layers teams skip.

exercises.prompt: About what share of agent projects never reach production?

facts.text: Mapped against the eight components, the tribunal is strong in some layers and weak in others: strong in memory/state and guardrails, weak in sensors and verification.

Memory/state is strong because it is files-only with a proven clean-session bootstrap; guardrails are strong because they are structural rules like `DeepSeek-once` and `MAX_LANES=4` the model cannot override.
Sensors are weak because they lean on byte counts — exactly the 'trivial check' the literature warns about. They confirm size, not correctness.

Verification is described as 'doctrine, not machinery' — the most-skipped layer. The tribunal relies on the habit of challenging and citing rather than an automated gate, which is both its strength and its gap.
In the learn path, the checkpoint asks you to name which layer the tribunal is weakest in — it is verification, the layer real agents skip.

exercises.prompt: Which layers of the tribunal are STRONGEST?
The tribunal's sensors are weak because:
options: byte count is the 'trivial check' the literature warns about
there are too many of them
they run on the wrong lane

exercises.prompt: The tribunal's verification was described as:

facts.text: The sensor gap is not theoretical — two live defects in the hub proved it. Sensors are the feedback layer, and these bugs slipped past because the checks were too shallow.
Defect 1: `class: lane-benchmark` auto-picked 5 lanes, blowing past `MAX_LANES=4` AND breaking the `DeepSeek-once` guard. The sensor never validated lane count against the guardrail.
Defect 2: `hub verdict` used substring match, so a slug that is a substring of another silently rewrote the wrong ledger row. A better sensor (exact match) would have caught it.
These look like cosmetic bugs, but both are precisely the sensor gap the statistics lesson warned about: shallow checks that pass while real harm slips through.

options: 5 lanes were auto-picked, failing MAX_LANES=4 and DeepSeek-once
substring match could rewrite the wrong ledger row

exercises.prompt: Why do these matter as a lesson?
options: both are exactly the sensor gap they prove
